title: Why Did the Bronze Age Collapse? (It Wasn't Just the Sea Peoples)

sentences.t: Around the year 1200 BC, the eastern Mediterranean was about as connected as the ancient world ever got.
You had the Egyptians, the Hittites, the Mycenaean Greeks, the Babylonians, all trading, writing letters, sending each other gifts.
And within maybe fifty years, almost all of it was gone.
Palaces burned, writing disappeared in Greece for centuries, and the Hittite empire basically vanished.
So what happened?
For a long time the answer was simple, the Sea Peoples.
We have Egyptian inscriptions describing invaders from the sea who swept through and destroyed everything in their path.
And for a long time historians took that more or less at face value.
But the more we dig, and I mean literally dig, the less that story works on its own.
Because a lot of these cities don't look like they were destroyed by one big invasion.
Some of them seem to have been abandoned slowly, and some were hit by earthquakes, and some were probably attacked by their own people.

Okay, back to 1177 BC.
Most historians today think it wasn't one cause, it was a whole bunch of them hitting at once.
Let's start with drought.
Pollen from lake beds and sediment cores suggests a long dry period across the region, lasting maybe a couple of centuries.
And we have letters from the time asking for grain, including one where the Hittite king is basically begging for a shipment, saying it's a matter of life or death.
Then earthquakes.
There seems to have been a run of big quakes over a few decades, which some researchers call an earthquake storm.
That on its own wouldn't end a civilization, but if your palace collapses during a famine, you might not rebuild it.
And then the trade network itself.
Bronze is copper plus tin, and the tin came from very far away, so if any link in that chain breaks, nobody can make bronze.
These kingdoms were so dependent on each other that when one wobbled, it pulled the others down with it.
And yes, there were raiders, the Sea Peoples are real, but they might be more of a symptom than the cause.
Some of them were probably displaced people, running from the same drought and famine, looking for somewhere to land.
So the picture we end up with is a system collapse, lots of problems at once, in a world that had become too interconnected to absorb them.
